readerTitle: Two bike shops, same sales, very different businesses
caseNote: 가상 사례 (자전거 매장 두 곳, 예약 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 매출은 하나의 숫자가 아니라 성격이 다른 수입 흐름들의 묶음이며, 같은 총매출도 흐름의 구성에 따라 전혀 다른 사업이 된다.
misconception: 매출 총액이 같으면 사업의 건강도도 비슷하다. 수입원은 많을수록 좋다.

sources.text: Osterwalder, A. & Pigneur, Y. (2010). Business Model Generation. 수익원(Revenue Streams)을 비즈니스 모델의 구성 요소로 설명

factChecks.note: 자전거 매장 계산: 평년 A $500k(자전거 판매 100%), B $300k + $140k + $60k = $500k. 부진한 해 자전거 판매 30% 감소 가정: A $350k(−30%), B $210k + $140k + $60k = $410k(−18%). 수리·서비스 플랜은 변하지 않는다고 단순화했습니다.
소프트웨어 사례: 설치비 $250k + 월 구독 $150k = $400k. 수치는 모두 가상입니다.

cards.title: Two bike shops, same sales, very different businesses
body: Two bike shops sit on the same street. Each took in $500,000 last year.
On paper they look like twins. Then a cold, wet spring arrives, and only one of them has a bad year.

image.label: Two identical bike shop fronts side by side
image.brief: 같은 거리에 나란히 선 자전거 매장 두 곳. 간판은 "Shop A", "Shop B"만 표기. 위에 비구름. 한쪽 매장 안에는 새 자전거만, 다른 쪽에는 새 자전거와 수리대, 공구가 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Which shop would you rather own?
body: **Shop A** earns all $500,000 from selling new bikes.
**Shop B** earns $300,000 from new bikes, $140,000 from repairs and $60,000 from yearly service plans that customers pay up front.
Both are for sale at the same price. Which do you buy?

options.text: Either one. The sales are the same
options.feedback: The totals match, but the money arrives in different ways. That difference shows up the moment conditions change.

options.text: Shop B, because its money comes in several different ways
options.feedback: Repairs and prepaid plans keep coming when people stop buying new bikes. You trade a simpler shop for a steadier one.

options.text: Can't say until I see the profit on each
options.feedback: Profit matters, and we'll get to it. But how the money comes in already tells you a lot about risk.

cards.title: New bike sales fell 30%. The shops did not fall equally.
body: In the slow year, people kept riding their old bikes and fixed them instead of replacing them.
Shop A lost 30% of its sales. Shop B lost 18%, because two of its three income sources didn't move.

cards.title: Revenue streams
body: A **revenue stream** is one distinct way money comes into a business: a specific thing you charge for, paid in a specific way.
Shop B has three streams. Each answers four questions differently: *what* is paid for, *how often*, *when* the money arrives, and *how predictable* it is.
Total sales is the sum. The streams are what you actually run.

image.label: Shop B's revenue split into three streams
image.brief: 세 개의 물줄기가 하나의 강으로 합쳐지는 일러스트. 각 물줄기 라벨: "New bikes $300k · one-off", "Repairs $140k · repeat", "Service plans $60k · paid up front". 강 끝에 "$500k".

cards.title: Each stream behaves differently.
body: Look at Shop B's three streams side by side:
list: **New bikes:** big tickets, rare, rises and falls with weather and the economy
**Repairs:** small tickets, frequent, needed whatever the weather
**Service plans:** paid before any work is done, easy to forecast
cards.callout: The streams also feed each other. Every bike sold today is a repair customer next year.

cards.title: Most businesses already have more than one stream.
body: A restaurant may earn from dine-in, delivery and catering. Catering is booked weeks ahead. Delivery depends on someone else's app.
A plumber earns from emergency call-outs and from yearly maintenance contracts. One pays well but is unpredictable. The other is smaller but steady.
cards.softwareNote: A software company might earn from setup fees, monthly subscriptions and paid add-ons. A setup fee is earned once. A subscription has to be earned again every month, but it keeps coming if customers stay.

cards.title: More streams is not automatically better.
body: Each stream needs its own skills, staff and attention. A bike shop that adds rentals, cafés and classes can end up doing all of them badly.
A small stream can also cost more to run than it brings in. And one stream can eat another: cheap service plans may replace repairs that paid more.
Add a stream when it fits what you already do well.

cards.title: Now it's a booking software company.
body: Your company sells booking software to salons. Last year it earned $400,000: $250,000 from one-time setup fees and $150,000 from monthly subscriptions.
You want a steadier business next year. Where do you focus?

options.text: Sign more new salons to grow setup fees
options.feedback: Setup fees bring cash fast, but each one is earned once. Next year starts from zero again.

options.text: Grow subscriptions, even if it means cutting the setup fee
options.feedback: You give up some cash today for money that repeats every month. Each salon that stays makes next year easier to predict.

options.text: Add ads, consulting and a hardware line
options.feedback: New streams spread a small team thin. Each one needs different skills before it earns anything.

cards.title: Don't read revenue as one number. Read it as streams.
body: The same total can hide a fragile business or a steady one. What matters is what you're paid for, how often, and how reliably.
**Try it today:** split last year's revenue into its streams. For each, note how often it repeats and what would make it drop.
